articles.title: Brush and eraser: size, hardness, opacity, smoothing
articles.summary: The Brush (B) and Eraser (E) paint or remove pixels on a layer, or paint a zone mask in ZONE mode. A handful of sliders control how the stroke feels.
articles.what: In ZONE mode the brush paints a mask that says where a zone applies. In LAYER mode it paints the selected layer's pixels. The current brush Size display is diameter in pixels: 2 to 600, default 40. Its stored slider value is radius 1 to 300, default 20; the SPB_TFX2_OFF compatibility display shows that stored value instead. Opacity is how see-through the paint is, 1 to 100% (default 100). Hardness is 0 for a soft feathered edge up to 100 for a hard edge. Flow is how fast paint builds up per pass. Spacing is the distance between dabs as a percent of brush size. Smoothing averages out hand jitter (default 10%). Stabilizer makes the tip trail the pointer like a lazy mouse, 0 to 200 px. Brush shape can be round, square, diamond, slash or noise, and Pattern Brush paints with a texture instead of a solid colour. The Eraser has three modes: Soft (brush), Hard (square block) or Clear Current Target. On the layer Brush, the Dynamics button next to Flow opens Brush dynamics: presets such as Speckle, Mud splatter, Dust and overspray, Confetti and Taper out. Shift-click a second point to draw a straight line, and it keeps the taper.
when: You want to hand-draw where a zone applies.
You are fixing artwork on a layer.
You overpainted and need to erase.
how: 1. Pick Brush (B) or Erase (E) in the tool row.
2. Check the ZONE | LAYER switch: ZONE paints a mask, LAYER paints pixels.
3. Set Size, Hardness and Opacity in the tool options bar. Use [ and ] to change size (the steps get bigger as the brush gets bigger) and { and } to change hardness.
4. Drag on the canvas. Press X to swap the paint colour with the background colour.
5. Switch the Eraser mode dropdown to Soft, Hard or Clear Current Target as needed.

tips: Number keys 1 to 9 set tool opacity to 10 to 90 percent, and 0 sets 100 percent.
Raise Smoothing or Stabilizer for long, steady lines.
The Spatial brush has its own size slider, 3 to 80 px.

When the selected zone has an area, a Clip to <zone> box appears in the tool options bar and is ticked. With it on, the Brush, the Eraser and the retouch tools only change pixels inside that zone, so painting red over the car numbers leaves them alone. Untick it to paint anywhere on the layer.
A Pattern Brush stays anchored to the canvas, so the texture does not slide along with the brush.
Each tool remembers its own size, hardness and opacity. Hold Alt and drag with the right mouse button on the canvas to change size (left or right) and hardness (up or down) without touching a slider.
Dynamics (next to Flow) makes every dab a little different: speckle, spray, splatter, random colours or a stroke that tapers to a point.
pitfalls: Block and Clear Target eraser modes are always full strength. Only Soft listens to opacity.
If the brush seems to do nothing, check you are in the right mode (ZONE or LAYER) and that a layer is selected.

deep.heading: How a stroke is built
deep.body: The brush does not draw a line. It stamps round dabs along your path. Spacing sets the gap between dabs as a percent of brush size (1 to 200, default 25), so a low number gives a smooth solid line and a high number gives a dotted one. Each dab is as strong as Opacity times Flow, so 50% Opacity with 50% Flow lands at about 25% strength per dab.

deep.heading: Smooth versus Stab
deep.body: Smooth (0 to 100, default 10) blends the pointer position with the average of your last 8 pointer samples. At 0 the tip follows your hand exactly. At 100 it sits on the average, which rounds wobble but also rounds corners. Stab (0 to 200 px, default 0) works like a rope: the tip stays put until the pointer is farther away than the rope length, then it is dragged behind. Use Smooth for natural lines and Stab for ruler-straight ones.

deep.heading: What the Eraser changes
deep.body: The Eraser has three modes in its dropdown. Soft (Brush) behaves like the brush and listens to Size, Opacity, Hard, Flow, Spacing, Smooth and Stab. Hard (Block) is a square that is always 100% opaque, so Opacity, Hard and Flow are hidden. Clear Current Target is a one-click command that wipes the whole zone mask or the whole selected layer, so it hides every brush control.

deep.heading: Keys that change the brush while you paint
deep.body: The [ key makes the brush 5 px smaller and ] makes it 5 px bigger, within the 1 to 300 range. Shift+[ and Shift+] (the { and } keys) change Hard by 10 at a time. Number keys 1 to 9 set Opacity to 10 through 90 percent and 0 sets 100. Hard-edge and Clear Target erasers ignore the number keys and the Hard keys, and the app shows a short message instead.

Strokes can be stepped back, so you can try a wide soft brush and undo it if it is wrong.
Every slider named here lives in the tool options bar, and which ones show depends on the tool and eraser mode.
Use the brush for fresh paint and the retouch tools to fix or blend what is already on the layer.

faq.q: Why do I not see Hard or Flow when I pick the eraser?
faq.a: Those sliders hide in the modes that ignore them. Hard (Block) hides Opacity, Hard and Flow. Clear Current Target hides almost everything. Switch the dropdown to Soft (Brush) to get them back.

faq.q: Do Opacity and Flow do the same thing?
faq.a: No, they multiply. Opacity is how strong each dab is and Flow scales it again, so 50% Opacity with 50% Flow lands at about 25% per dab. Lower Flow is good for airbrush build-up.

faq.q: How do I draw a straight line?
faq.a: Click once to start, then hold Shift and click where it should end. The line runs from the end of your last stroke on the same layer or zone.

faq.q: How big can the brush get?
faq.a: The current Brush/Eraser size display is diameter, 2 to 600 px (default 40). The underlying slider stores radius, 1 to 300 (default 20); the SPB_TFX2_OFF compatibility display uses that stored value. The spatial region brush has a separate 3 to 80 px slider.

faq.q: What does the X key do?
faq.a: It swaps the foreground and background colours so you can flip between two paint colours without opening a picker.

faq.q: The number keys did nothing on the eraser. Why?
faq.a: Hard (Block) is always 100% opaque and Clear Current Target has no opacity at all. Choose Soft (Brush) and the number keys work again.

faq.q: Is there a way to paint with a texture?
faq.a: Yes. Pick a Pattern Brush from the dropdown: Carbon Fiber, Metal Flake, Crosshatch, Brushed Metal, Canvas Weave or Random Noise. Solid Color goes back to plain paint.

faq.q: How do I make a speckled, sprayed or tapered stroke?
faq.a: Pick the Brush in LAYER mode and click Dynamics next to Flow. Choose Speckle, Dust and overspray, Mud splatter or Taper out.

mistakes.symptom: The brush seems to do nothing
mistakes.cause: You are in the wrong mode, or LAYER mode has no layer selected.
mistakes.fix: Look at the ZONE | LAYER switch. In LAYER mode click a layer first. If none can be painted, add a blank layer.

mistakes.symptom: My line looks dotted
mistakes.cause: Spacing is set high, so the dabs are placed far apart.
mistakes.fix: Bring Spacing back toward the default 25 percent, or lower for thin lines.

mistakes.symptom: Long lines have rounded corners and lag
mistakes.cause: Smooth or Stab is very high. Both pull the tip away from the pointer.
mistakes.fix: Lower them for detail work, and raise them only for long straight or gentle curves.

mistakes.symptom: The eraser removed everything in one click
mistakes.cause: Clear Current Target is a wipe command, not a brush.
mistakes.fix: Press Ctrl+Z to undo, then change the Eraser mode dropdown to Soft (Brush).

protips: Press X to swap colours, [ and ] to resize, and the number keys for opacity, so your hand never leaves the canvas.
For a ruler-straight stripe use Stab around 40 px instead of a shaky Shift+click retry: the tip lags behind your pointer and straightens the path.
Shift+click lines work for several paint tools, not just the brush, so you can chain straight segments by clicking corner to corner.

articles.title: Fill bucket
articles.summary: The Fill bucket (K) fills a closed region of a zone mask or a layer in one click.
articles.what: In ZONE mode it fills a region of the zone's mask. In LAYER mode it fills pixels on the selected layer, using either a solid colour or a baked Special finish, chosen with the Layer Brush / Fill paint source dropdown. Number keys set its opacity on layers. Two keyboard fills work on a selection: Alt+Backspace fills with the foreground colour and Ctrl+Backspace with the background colour. The message after a fill counts the pixels that really changed. If you click outside an active selection, it says that spot is outside the active selection and nothing is filled. For fades between colours, use the Gradient tool instead.
when: You need to fill a closed shape with colour.
You want a layer area to carry a finish look instead of flat colour.
how: Choose Fill (K), then check the Zone / Layer toolbar switch and the intended target. Zone mode fills the selected Zone mask; Layer mode fills the selected editable layer pixels.
For a layer fill, set the foreground colour, or select Special (Baked) and Choose Special in the layer paint-source controls. Set tolerance, Contiguous and opacity for the intended result.
Click inside the area and inside any active selection. A click outside the active selection fills nothing. Read the changed-pixel result instead of assuming the entire visible car was edited.
Use Ctrl+Z if the result is wrong. For a fade between colours, use the separate Gradient tool.

Fill is meant for closed areas, so check the outline has no gaps before you click.

deep.heading: What counts as the same colour
deep.body: The bucket looks at the pixel you click, then floods outward to every pixel whose red, green and blue are close to it. Closeness is measured as straight-line distance in colour, not per channel. Tolerance runs 0 to 255 with a default of 32, and a tolerance of 32 allows roughly 55 points of total colour distance. At 0 only the exact same colour is taken, which is right for flat artwork. Raise it for photos, gradients and anti-aliased edges.

deep.heading: Contiguous and Sample
deep.body: Contiguous is on by default and keeps the fill to pixels that touch the one you clicked. Turn it off and the bucket grabs every matching pixel on the whole sheet, even in islands you cannot see touching. Beside it the bar shows what is being matched: Sample: Active Layer in LAYER mode, Sample: Composite in ZONE mode, where it reads the visible source paint underneath your zones.

deep.heading: Zone fill versus layer fill
deep.body: In ZONE mode the bucket writes into the selected zone's mask, and the Selection Mode dropdown decides how: Add keeps what was there, Replace starts the mask over, Subtract removes the matched area. If the result would change nothing, the app says the fill was skipped. In LAYER mode it paints real pixels on the layer, using Solid Color or Special (Baked) from the paint source dropdown, and the Opacity slider controls how strongly.

After a bucket fill, grow, shrink or feather the result to close hairline gaps.
The fill tolerance works on the same colour-distance idea as zone colour tolerance, so what grabs cleanly in one grabs cleanly in the other.
Check the ZONE | LAYER switch first: the bucket edits a mask in one and real pixels in the other.

faq.q: Why did the bucket fill the whole car?
faq.a: Tolerance is too high for the area, or Contiguous is off. Drop Tolerance toward 10 to 32 and tick Contiguous.

faq.q: Why did it leave a rim around my shape?
faq.a: Edges are anti-aliased, so the rim pixels are a blend of two colours outside the tolerance. Raise Tolerance a little or grow the result by a pixel or two.

faq.q: What does the Fill button in the selection bar do?
faq.a: It is a different thing. It closes holes inside a selection. The bucket tool floods a colour region.

faq.q: Can I fill with a finish, not just a colour?
faq.a: On a layer, yes. Change the paint source dropdown to Special (Baked), press Choose Special, then click.

faq.q: I clicked and nothing happened.
faq.a: The fill would not change anything, or the layer is locked or not selected. A short message tells you which. Pick a different spot or unlock the layer.

faq.q: How do I fill a selection without clicking?
faq.a: Make a selection, then press Alt+Backspace to fill with the foreground colour or Ctrl+Backspace for the background colour.

faq.q: It says that spot is outside the active selection.
faq.a: You clicked outside your selection, so nothing was filled. Click inside the selection, or clear it with Ctrl+D.

faq.q: Where is the gradient tool?
faq.a: Press G (Shift+G switches between Gradient and Fill) or open the Retouch menu. The Colours button next to Linear and Reverse has presets and colour stops. See the Gradient article.

mistakes.symptom: The fill leaks across the whole panel
mistakes.cause: There is a gap in the outline, or Tolerance is so high that the border colour counts as a match.
mistakes.fix: Undo with Ctrl+Z, lower Tolerance, and close the gap with the brush before filling again.

mistakes.symptom: Only a speckled part of the area is filled
mistakes.cause: Tolerance is too low for noisy or gradient artwork.
mistakes.fix: Raise Tolerance in steps of 10 until the whole area is taken.

mistakes.symptom: A zone fill adds to the old mask instead of replacing it
mistakes.cause: Selection Mode is on Mode: Add (+), the default.
mistakes.fix: Switch the dropdown to Mode: Replace before clicking.

mistakes.symptom: The same colour on a logo got caught too
mistakes.cause: Contiguous is off, or the logo touches the body at the same colour.
mistakes.fix: Turn Contiguous on, and restrict the zone to a layer or box if the colours truly touch.

mistakes.symptom: Fill skipped: that spot is outside the active selection
mistakes.cause: Your click was outside the selection.
mistakes.fix: Click inside it, or clear the selection with Ctrl+D.

protips: Tolerance 0 plus Contiguous on is a perfect picker for flat vector-style artwork, and anything else you click stays untouched.
The bucket matches against the colour of the exact pixel you click, so click in the middle of a flat area, not on an anti-aliased edge.
Switch Selection Mode to Mode: Subtract and click to carve a matching colour back out of a zone mask.

articles.title: Eyedropper (Color) and Pick Item
articles.summary: Color (I) samples paint. An armed PICK COLOR FROM CAR, an open Zone popout, or Zone mode can send that sample to the selected Zone; unarmed Layer mode with the popout closed sets the foreground swatch. Pick Item (Y) isolates connected artwork instead.
articles.what: Color (I) samples paint. An armed PICK COLOR FROM CAR, an open Zone popout, or Zone mode can send that sample to the selected Zone; unarmed Layer mode with the popout closed sets the foreground swatch. Pick Item (Y) isolates connected artwork instead. + Add Color stacks shades; Set replaces the Zone colour list. Shift+click or Current Layer samples the active layer. Alt+click temporarily samples the foreground only when the current tool does not own Alt.
when: You want a zone to catch one colour on the paint.
You need to move just one logo on a layer with many.
how: Decide whether you need a Zone colour match or a brush foreground. For a Zone, select the intended Zone and arm PICK COLOR FROM CAR, then choose Color (I).
Click the colour on the canvas. Check the selected Zone and its colour chips: an armed picker or open Zone popout can commit the colour even while the toolbar shows Layer mode.
Use + Add Color to keep several shades. Set replaces the list with the sampled colour. Each chip uses the Zone picker tolerance, or 40 when that setting is absent.

For a foreground-only sample, use temporary Alt+click with a tool that does not use Alt itself. With Color (I), use unarmed Layer mode and close the Zone popout; Shift+click or Current Layer samples only the active layer.

deep.heading: What a click does
deep.body: Color reads Point, 3x3, 5x5 or 11x11 samples from All Layers or Current Layer. An armed PICK COLOR FROM CAR, an open Zone popout, or Zone mode can commit to the current selected Zone. Layer mode alone does not prevent that commit. With no Zone commit route, it updates the foreground swatch. New chips inherit the Zone picker tolerance; absent a setting, the fallback is 40.

deep.heading: Add Color, Set and the colour stack
deep.body: + Add Color stacks the last picked colour onto the zone, so one zone can hold several shades of the same paint. A colour already in the zone is refused with a message. Set does the opposite: it replaces everything with this single colour and clears the stack. Each stacked colour carries its own tolerance, so a loose shade and an exact shade can live in one zone.

deep.heading: Alt and Shift while sampling
deep.body: Holding Alt and clicking with most tools grabs the colour under the cursor as your foreground colour, adds it to recent colours and shows Sampled with the hex value. Tools that use Alt for something else, such as Clone, Healing, Shape, Pen and the marquees, keep their own Alt behaviour. With the Color tool, Shift+click samples only the active layer instead of the whole picture, which ignores whatever sits above it.

deep.heading: Pick Item is not a colour tool
deep.body: Pick Item (Y) picks a thing, not a colour. In LAYER mode it draws a tight box around one sponsor, number or shape inside a layer so you can move or rotate just that piece. In ZONE mode it picks a spec pattern piece to move on its own.

faq.q: What starting tolerance does a picked colour get?
faq.a: The selected Zone's picker tolerance is used for the new colour chip; the fallback is 40 if that setting is absent. Check each chip's tolerance rather than assuming every Zone starts at 40.

faq.q: Why does it say a colour is already in the zone?
faq.a: Colours are compared by exact hex value and a repeat is refused. Pick a slightly different shade or raise the tolerance on the existing colour.

faq.q: What is the difference between + Add Color and Set?
faq.a: + Add Color stacks another colour on the zone. Set swaps the whole list for this one colour.

faq.q: How do I grab a colour without leaving my brush?
faq.a: Hold Alt and click. The colour becomes your foreground colour and joins the recent colours. It does not work with tools that use Alt for other jobs, such as Clone and Healing.

faq.q: Can I sample only one layer?
faq.a: Yes. Select the layer, use the Color tool and Shift+click. It ignores the paint and other layers around it.

faq.q: Pick Item grabbed the whole layer. Why?
faq.a: Pick Item isolates one connected piece of artwork. If a number touches a stripe in the same layer they count as one piece, so cut them onto separate layers first.

mistakes.symptom: The zone grabs the logo as well as the body
mistakes.cause: Both use the same colour, and a colour pick has no sense of place.
mistakes.fix: Add a box, lasso or layer restriction to the zone, or use Exclude to paint the logo out of the match.

mistakes.symptom: Edges stay unpainted around the shape
mistakes.cause: Anti-aliased edge pixels are blends that sit outside the tolerance.
mistakes.fix: Slide Color Match toward Loose, or add the edge shade with + Add Color.

mistakes.symptom: I clicked and the zone did not change
mistakes.cause: No zone was selected, or the colour was already in it.
mistakes.fix: Select a zone in the left column first, then click again. A duplicate is refused on purpose.

protips: Alt+click works as a temporary eyedropper from almost any painting tool, so you can match colours without switching tools.
Use the Sample dropdown on 5x5 or 11x11 for noisy or speckled paint so one stray pixel does not become your colour.
Shift+click lets you pull a clean colour from one layer even when other layers cover it on screen.

articles.title: Retouch tools: Color Brush, Recolor, Healing, Clone, Smudge, Burn and more
articles.summary: The RETOUCH menu holds the pixel tools for fixing and painting artwork on a layer: Color Brush, Recolor, Healing Brush, Clone Stamp, Smudge, Blur, Sharpen, Dodge, Burn, Pencil, History Brush and Gradient.
articles.what: Color Brush (C) paints a solid colour or pattern brush onto the selected layer. Recolor (Shift+B, twice) paints a new hue over a sampled colour. Healing Brush (J) takes clean texture from a source you pick with Alt+click, then paints it into the target. Smudge (Q) smears layer pixels in the drag direction. Burn (Shift+O) darkens the pixels under the brush. They work on layer pixels, so they need LAYER mode and a layer to paint on; the menu is greyed out until a blank layer exists, which the "+ Add blank for Color Brush" button creates. The menu also holds Clone Stamp (S), Blur (R), Sharpen (R twice), Dodge (O), Pencil (Shift+B), History Brush (Shift+Y) and Gradient (G). The Healing Brush matches the colours around the spot, so the repair blends in without seams. Sharpen works, and the Blur radius follows the brush size.
when: You need to touch up a sponsor, number or decal.
The Color Brush is greyed out.
how: 1. Switch to LAYER mode and select the layer you want to fix.
2. Open RETOUCH in the toolbar. If it is greyed, press "+ Add blank for Color Brush" first.
3. Pick the tool. Set its size and strength in the tool options bar.
4. For Healing, press Set source and click a clean area (Alt+click also picks it), then paint over the flaw.
5. Undo with Ctrl+Z if you do not like it.

deep.heading: Recolor changes hue, not light
deep.body: Recolor samples the colour under the cursor when you start a stroke. Only pixels within Tolerance of that sampled colour are touched (Tolerance defaults to 32 and is the same slider the wand uses). They are pushed toward your foreground colour while keeping their own lightness, so shading, scratches and texture survive. Pixels near the edge of the tolerance get a weaker change, which gives a soft transition instead of a hard cut.

deep.heading: Burn builds up slowly on purpose
deep.body: Burn darkens a little with every dab. Exposure runs 1 to 100 percent with a default of 20, and the tonal range dropdown picks Shadows, Midtones (the default) or Highlights, which decides which pixels react most. Each dab also multiplies by Flow and by the brush edge falloff, so at the defaults one pass is a gentle nudge. Pixels that are fully transparent are skipped, and black can never go darker.

deep.heading: Smudge and Healing
deep.body: Smudge picks up the colour under the brush and drags it along your stroke. Its Strength runs 1 to 100 percent with a default of 50, and the dab is also scaled by Flow. Healing Brush copies texture from a source point you set with Alt+click or the Set source button. With Aligned on (the default) the source follows your cursor across strokes. With Aligned off every new stroke starts again from the point you sampled.

deep.heading: Selections protect the rest of the layer
deep.body: If a pixel selection is active, Color Brush, Recolor, Smudge and Burn all stay inside it. A selection with a soft edge gives your retouch a soft edge too.

faq.q: Why is the whole Retouch menu greyed out?
faq.a: These brushes paint on a layer. A flat car image has none, so press + Add blank for Color Brush or open a layered file.

faq.q: What is the difference between Color Brush and Recolor?
faq.a: Color Brush paints a flat colour or a pattern on top. Recolor swaps the hue of existing colour and keeps the lightness and texture.

faq.q: Why does Recolor miss some pixels?
faq.a: Only pixels near the colour you first clicked change. Raise Tolerance to include more shades.

faq.q: How do I set the healing source?
faq.a: Alt+click a clean spot, or press Set source and then click. The bar shows Source not set until you do, and Clear source resets it.

faq.q: Can I use Burn on the whole car paint?
faq.a: No. Burn works on layer pixels. Use zone finishes and base settings for car-wide darkening.

faq.q: Do the number keys work here?
faq.a: Yes. They set the strength of the active tool, such as Smudge strength or Burn exposure.

mistakes.symptom: Recolor turned everything muddy
mistakes.cause: Tolerance is very high, so far-off colours are pulled in too.
mistakes.fix: Undo with Ctrl+Z, lower Tolerance, and sample a cleaner starting colour.

mistakes.symptom: Burn does almost nothing
mistakes.cause: Exposure is low and the tone range does not match the pixels you are painting.
mistakes.fix: Raise Exposure or pick the tonal range that matches the area, then do a few passes.

mistakes.symptom: The healing patch shows a visible copy
mistakes.cause: The source sits next to a different tone, or Aligned is off.
mistakes.fix: Pick a source with similar tone and keep Aligned on for long strokes.

mistakes.symptom: Nothing happens at all with these tools
mistakes.cause: No layer is selected, or it is locked.
mistakes.fix: Select an unlocked layer in LAYER mode. Press + Add blank for Color Brush if you have none.

protips: Recolor keeps lightness, so it is the right tool to restyle a logo without losing its 3D look; a Color Brush stroke would flatten it.
Burn is deliberately weak per pass. Treat it like an airbrush and build shadow with several light passes.
A feathered selection around the area you want to fix gives the retouch a soft edge for free.

articles.title: Marquee, Lasso, Magic Wand and other selection tools
articles.summary: Selection tools decide which pixels you are about to work on. Pick the one that fits the shape: box, circle, free-hand, colour or edge.
articles.what: Rect (M) drags a box selection and the Elliptical Marquee (M, twice) drags an oval, with Shift pressed during the drag for a circle and Alt pressed during the drag to draw from the centre. Lasso (L) draws a free-hand outline; press Enter or return near the start to close it. The Magic Wand (W) selects similar colours. Select All Color (A) selects every pixel of a sampled colour across the whole paint. Grab Object (Shift+W) selects a whole number or logo outline with one click. Smart Region Fill selects an area bounded by edges, and Edge Preview shows the detected boundaries in red so you can adjust tolerance first. Shift held when you start a Rect or Ellipse drag adds to the selection and Alt held at the start subtracts; pressed after the drag has started, Shift makes a square or circle and Alt draws from the centre. Esc cancels the drag.
when: You want a zone to cover one panel or an odd shape.
You want to select a stripe, number or logo.
how: Select the Zone that should hold the selection. If you intend to edit artwork afterward, also choose the intended editable Layer and check the toolbar mode after changing tools. Selection tools use the Zone mask even when started from Layer mode.
Choose Wand (W) for a touching area, Select All Color (A) for matching pixels across the sheet, or a marquee/lasso for a drawn region. Set tolerance and Contiguous before clicking.

Click to replace the selection. Shift at the start adds and Alt at the start subtracts. For a marquee, pressing Shift after dragging starts constrains its shape; Alt after dragging starts uses its centre.
For a rough outline, open Mask > Refine Edge after making a nonempty selection. Review the preview and output choice; it is not committed until Apply.

For material coverage, use the current selection with the intended Zone. For Layer painting, verify the editable Layer and Layer mode; supported tools can return there after a Layer-to-selection hop while preserving the selection.

Rect and Ellipse marquee: Shift or Alt held at the start add or subtract. Shift or Alt pressed after you start dragging make a square or circle and draw from the centre. Esc cancels.
pitfalls: The wand grabs far-away bits when Contiguous is off.
Grab Object works best on clear solid shapes.
M picks the Rectangle marquee. Press M again for the Elliptical Marquee.

deep.heading: Selections belong to the selected zone
deep.body: In ZONE mode every selection tool writes into the mask of the zone selected on the left, so pick the zone first. With none selected the tool says to select a zone and does nothing. Each successful selection is one undo step, and a selection that would change nothing is skipped with a message instead of cluttering your history.

deep.heading: How the Wand measures closeness
deep.body: The Wand takes the colour under your click, averaged over the Sample area: Point Sample, 3x3 Average (the default), 5x5 Average or 11x11 Average. A pixel matches when none of its red, green, blue or transparency values is further from that sample than Tolerance, which runs 0 to 255 and defaults to 32. This is a per-channel limit, so it is stricter than the Fill bucket, which measures colour distance in a straight line.

deep.heading: Contiguous, Select All Color and Anti Alias
deep.body: With Contiguous on, the Wand only spreads to touching pixels. Select All Color is the same idea with Contiguous forced off, so it collects every matching pixel anywhere on the sheet. Anti Alias adds a soft rim of partly selected pixels just outside the tolerance, a band of 4 to 32 levels wide that grows with Tolerance, so edges are not jagged.

deep.heading: Shape tools and their modifier keys
deep.body: Rect (M) drags a box: Shift or Alt held at the start add or subtract, Shift pressed mid-drag makes a square, Alt pressed mid-drag draws from the centre and Esc cancels. Elliptical Marquee (M, twice) does the same for ovals, with Shift for a circle. Lasso (L) either drags freehand and closes on release, or you click polygon points and press Enter or double-click to close, with Backspace removing the last point. For the Wand, Select All Color, Grab Object and Smart Region Fill, Shift adds to the selection and Alt subtracts.

faq.q: Why does the Wand say to select a zone?
faq.a: Selection tools hold their mask on the selected Zone, including a selection started from Layer mode, so select a valid Zone first. This does not mean a Wand click paints that Zone or edits layer pixels. For later Layer painting, check the intended editable Layer and the toolbar mode; the supported return-to-Layer path preserves a valid selection.

faq.q: What is the difference between Wand and Select All Color?
faq.a: The Wand follows touching pixels when Contiguous is on. Select All Color always ignores contact and picks matching pixels everywhere.

faq.q: How do I add to a selection without changing the mode dropdown?
faq.a: Hold Shift while you click or drag. Hold Alt to subtract.

faq.q: What does Grab Object do?
faq.a: Click inside a solid part of a number or logo and it selects the whole shape including its outline and shadow. Hide wire or template guide layers first if they split the artwork.

faq.q: What is Smart Region Fill?
faq.a: It selects an area bounded by detected edges. Tolerance changes how sensitive the boundary detection is, and Edge Preview shows the boundaries in red.

faq.q: Which key is the rectangle marquee?
faq.a: M. Press M again to switch to the Elliptical Marquee. O is Dodge now.

faq.q: How do I make a perfect square or circle selection?
faq.a: Start the Rect or Ellipse marquee drag, then press and hold Shift while you drag. Alt pressed during the drag draws from the centre.

faq.q: How do I clean up a rough selection around a logo?
faq.a: Make a nonempty Wand, Lasso or Marquee selection, then open Mask > Refine Edge. Review the live preview and choose selection output or a cut-out layer. Nothing is final until Apply, and changing the selected Zone or its selection while the panel is open closes it.

mistakes.fix: Undo, tick Contiguous and lower Tolerance toward 10 to 32.

mistakes.symptom: The selection edge looks jagged
mistakes.cause: Anti Alias is off or the area is noisy.
mistakes.fix: Turn Anti Alias on and use 5x5 Average for noisy paint, or feather the result a few pixels.

mistakes.symptom: My lasso line will not close

mistakes.fix: Press Enter or double-click, and use Backspace to remove a misplaced point.

protips: Shift+click and Alt+click override whatever Selection Mode is set to, so you can add or subtract on the fly.
Wand Tolerance counts the transparency value too, so a semi-transparent edge is judged on both colour and see-through level.
The SELECT menu has Move Selection Border: arrow keys nudge the outline 1 px (10 px with Shift) and the pixels underneath do not move, so you can line a selection up exactly.

articles.title: Selection modes: Add, Replace, Subtract
articles.summary: The Selection mode dropdown decides whether a new selection adds to, replaces or removes from the one you already have.
articles.what: Add (+) joins the new area to the existing selection. Replace throws the old selection away and keeps only the new one. Subtract (-) cuts the new area out of the existing selection. With the wand you can also hold Shift to add and Alt to subtract without opening the dropdown.
when: The wand or lasso added when you wanted to replace.
You want to carve a hole out of a selection.
how: 1. Pick a selection tool.
2. Open the Selection mode dropdown in the tool options bar.
3. Choose Add, Replace or Subtract.
4. Make your next selection. Or hold Shift (add) or Alt (subtract) while you click with the wand.

controls.label: Selection mode dropdown (Add / Replace / Subtract)
controls.effect: How a new selection combines with the existing one: Add (+), Replace, Subtract.

tips: Use Subtract with a lasso to cut out a window or a number from a big selection.
pitfalls: If every new selection seems to pile onto the last one, the mode is on Add. Switch to Replace.

deep.heading: The mode resets when you switch tools
deep.body: The dropdown offers Mode: Add (+), Mode: Replace and Mode: Subtract (-). Each time you pick Lasso, Pen, Rect, Elliptical Marquee, Wand, Select All Color or Smart Region Fill, the app sets it back to Replace. A mode you chose for one tool does not follow you to the next. Fill and Gradient in ZONE mode also use this dropdown, but they do not reset it, so they act on whatever is showing.

deep.heading: Shift and Alt are one-gesture overrides
deep.body: For Wand, Select All Color, Smart Region Fill and Lasso, holding Shift while you click adds and holding Alt subtracts, whatever the dropdown says. The Pen is different: Shift snaps a segment to 45 degrees and Alt breaks the handles, and the finished path follows only the dropdown. Rect and Elliptical Marquee are different: there Shift means square or circle, Alt means draw from the centre and Esc cancels, so use the dropdown for add and subtract. A hint line next to the dropdown always shows the keys for the active tool.

deep.heading: What each mode does to the mask
deep.body: Add merges the new shape into the zone's current region. Replace swaps the whole region for the new shape, and Ctrl+Z gives the old region back. Subtract removes the new shape from the region, and if nothing in the region overlaps the app says no matching pixels and changes nothing.

faq.q: Why did my mode jump back to Replace?

faq.q: Shift makes a square with Rect. How do I add then?

faq.q: How do I remove a bit from a selection?
faq.a: Pick Mode: Subtract (-) and draw over the part to remove. With the Wand or Lasso you can just hold Alt.

faq.q: Can I undo a Replace?
faq.a: Yes. The old region is saved first, so Ctrl+Z brings it back.

faq.q: Do these modes affect layers too?
faq.a: The modes shape a zone's region. In LAYER mode a pixel selection controls where your brush and retouch tools work.

mistakes.symptom: Every new selection piles onto the last one
mistakes.cause: The dropdown is on Mode: Add (+), or you are using Fill or Gradient, which keep the current mode.
mistakes.fix: Choose Mode: Replace before you select.

mistakes.cause: Mode: Replace discards the old region.
mistakes.fix: Press Ctrl+Z, then switch to Mode: Add (+).

mistakes.symptom: Subtract did nothing
mistakes.cause: The shape you drew does not overlap the current region.
mistakes.fix: Draw over the part that is already selected.

protips: Holding Shift or Alt overrides the dropdown only for that one click, so you can keep Replace as your safe default and add on demand.
Fill and Gradient follow this dropdown too, which means you can subtract a gradient from a region the same way you subtract a lasso.

articles.title: Grow, shrink, feather, invert and mirror a selection
articles.summary: Once you have a selection or zone mask, a few buttons clean up the edge: grow, shrink, fill holes, feather, smooth, invert, copy and mirror.
articles.what: These are in the MASK menu and in the selection bar under the canvas. Grow and Shrink move the edge by 1 or 2 px. Fill Holes includes empty islands completely enclosed by the selection. Feather 2 px softens the edge. Smooth Edges removes jagged boundaries. Invert Mask swaps selected and unselected areas. Copy Mask sends this zone's mask to another zone, and Mirror Mask flips it horizontally. The Auto-feather box (0 to 50 px, default 0) softens the edge of the next selection you commit so the finish fades in at the border. Move Selection Border shifts the outline without moving pixels: Arrow moves 1 px and Shift+Arrow 10 px. Refine Edge... (MASK menu, under Smooth Edges) is the picture-aware version: it snaps the edge to the real outline of a logo or number and can make a clean cut-out layer. Copy and Cut follow the soft edge of a feathered selection, so a feathered Layer via Copy fades out instead of ending hard.
when: A zone edge is jagged, has pinholes or leaves a fringe of the old colour.
You want the finish to fade out at the edge instead of cutting off.
how: 1. Make a selection with any selection tool.
2. Open the MASK menu (or use the selection bar) and press Grow 2 px to add a safety edge around lettering.
3. Press Fill Holes if small islands inside the selection are missing.
4. Press Smooth Edges or Feather 2 px to soften.
5. Use Invert Mask to select everything else.

deep.heading: Grow and Shrink are pixel moves
deep.body: The buttons move the whole edge of the zone region by exactly 1 or 2 pixels, one pixel step at a time. Pressing a button twice is the same as moving 2 px. Grow stops at the canvas border and Shrink on an empty region says so. Nothing is recoloured; only the mask changes, and each press is one undo step.

deep.heading: Smooth Edges is a shrink then a grow
deep.body: Smooth Edges shrinks the region by 1 px and grows it back by 1 px. That erases hairline spurs and single-pixel specks and rounds tiny jagged steps, but it also removes any feature thinner than about 2 px, so thin pinstripes can vanish. Fill Holes does the opposite job: it fills empty islands completely enclosed by the region.

deep.heading: Feather is a blur of the mask
deep.body: Feather 2 px blurs the edge so the finish fades instead of ending on a line. Because a blur spreads both ways, the old hard edge ends up at about half strength, with fully strong coverage pulling back inside. If you need full strength right up to the original edge, press Grow 2 px first, then Feather 2 px. The Auto-feather box in the selection bar (0 to 50 px, default 0) does the same to the next selection you commit, and one undo reverts the whole selection.

deep.heading: Invert, copy and move
deep.body: Invert Mask swaps selected and unselected pixels. Ctrl+Shift+I inverts from the keyboard. Move Selection Border nudges the outline: Arrow moves 1 px and Shift+Arrow 10 px, and the pixels do not move.

faq.q: How far can I grow a selection?
faq.a: The Grow 1 px and Grow 2 px buttons add that much per press. Press them repeatedly to go further.

faq.q: Why did Smooth Edges delete my thin stripe?
faq.a: It shrinks by one pixel then grows back, so anything under about 2 px wide disappears. Skip Smooth Edges for fine lines.

faq.q: How do I fade a finish into the paint?
faq.a: Use Feather 2 px on an existing region, or set the Auto-feather box before you make the selection.

faq.q: What does Fill Holes fill?
faq.a: Only empty areas completely surrounded by the selection. Gaps that touch the outside edge are not holes.

faq.q: Can I undo a refine?
faq.a: Yes, each button press is one undo step with Ctrl+Z.

faq.q: Does feathering shrink my selection?
faq.a: It softens it. The old edge ends up at about half strength and the solid core pulls in slightly. Grow first if you want full strength at the old edge.

faq.q: Does Copy or Cut follow a feathered edge?
faq.a: Yes. Copy, Cut and Layer via Copy or Cut now follow the soft edge, so the new layer fades out instead of ending hard.

faq.q: What is the difference between Feather and Refine Edge?

articles.title: ZONE mode and LAYER mode: zone mask and layer
articles.summary: The ZONE | LAYER switch changes what every tool edits: where a finish applies (ZONE) or the artwork pixels (LAYER).
articles.what: A zone mask is the shape that says which pixels a zone owns. Painting or selecting in ZONE mode changes that shape; it never changes your artwork. A layer is real artwork (body paint, numbers, sponsors, tape). In LAYER mode, Brush, Erase, Move and the retouch tools change those pixels. The same tool does different things in the two modes: Brush paints a mask in ZONE mode and pixels in LAYER mode, and Transform moves the zone's pattern or base in ZONE mode but the selected artwork in LAYER mode.

You are not sure whether you are changing the finish area or the artwork.

2. Click ZONE to edit where finishes apply, or LAYER to edit artwork.
3. Then pick your tool.
4. To aim a zone at a layer, press MAKE ZONE on the layer card or Lock Zone (Ctrl+L).

deep.heading: Two switches, one toolbar
deep.body: The ZONE and LAYER buttons sit at the top of the toolbar. The tooltips say it plainly: in ZONE mode toolbar tools edit zones and masks only, and in LAYER mode they edit the selected layer only. ZONE is the starting mode. The active button glows green. When you switch, a short message names what the tools will now touch, such as the zone name or the selected layer.

deep.heading: What a zone mask is
deep.body: A zone mask is a map of pixels the zone owns. A finish is painted wherever the mask says. Brushing, selecting, filling or growing a mask never changes your source artwork, which is why ZONE mode is safe to experiment in. Pixel tools in LAYER mode are the opposite: they rewrite real pixels on a layer, and only Ctrl+Z gets them back.

deep.heading: Wrong-mode warnings
deep.body: Some tools only make sense in one mode. Text and Shape create a new layer, so they warn that they only work in LAYER mode. Fill, Retouch, Healing and similar pixel tools say they only edit layers in LAYER mode. Zone tools such as the zone Wand say they are zone tools and ask you to switch to ZONE. If you are in LAYER mode with no editable layer selected, the tool tells you why instead of silently doing nothing.

deep.heading: Same tool, different job
deep.body: Brush and Erase paint the mask in ZONE mode and pixels in LAYER mode. Fill floods a mask region in ZONE mode and fills layer pixels with colour or a baked Special in LAYER mode. Transform moves the zone's pattern or base in ZONE mode but the selected artwork in LAYER mode. Rect and Lasso make a zone region in ZONE mode and a pixel selection in LAYER mode.

faq.q: Which mode am I in?
faq.a: The active button, ZONE or LAYER, glows green at the top of the toolbar, and the tool options bar changes with it.

faq.q: I painted but my artwork did not change.
faq.a: You were in ZONE mode, so you painted a mask. Switch to LAYER and select a layer to paint pixels.

faq.q: I painted and now the finish looks wrong.
faq.a: In LAYER mode you changed pixels, not a zone. Press Ctrl+Z, then use ZONE mode to change where a finish applies.

faq.q: Why does Move not work?
faq.a: Move needs a selected layer. Switch to LAYER, select the layer, then drag.

faq.q: Which mode should a beginner stay in?
faq.a: ZONE. It only edits where finishes apply and never damages your artwork.

faq.q: Can the same selection be used in both modes?
faq.a: A selection made in ZONE mode becomes the zone's region. In LAYER mode a pixel selection limits where brush and retouch tools work.

faq.q: Is a zone more like a mask or like a layer, coming from Photoshop?
faq.a: A zone is closest to a mask plus a finish assignment: it picks pixels and says what look they get. Layers come from your PSD. The ZONE | LAYER switch is zone mode versus layer mode: ZONE edits where a finish applies, LAYER edits the artwork pixels.

mistakes.symptom: A tool shows a warning and nothing changes
mistakes.cause: The tool belongs to the other mode.
mistakes.fix: Click ZONE or LAYER as the message says and try again.

mistakes.symptom: I cannot paint in LAYER mode
mistakes.cause: No editable layer is selected, the layer is locked, or the file is a flat image with no layers.
mistakes.fix: Select an unlocked layer. For a flat file add a blank layer first.

mistakes.symptom: I edited a template guide
mistakes.cause: Layers named Mask, Wire or Car_Mandatory are guides, not artwork.
mistakes.fix: Undo and select the real artwork layer instead.

protips: Ctrl+L locks a zone to the selected layer, which is the quickest way to move from fixing artwork to styling it.
Hover the glowing button: the tooltip states exactly which kind of thing the toolbar will edit in that mode.
When something looks wrong after painting, check the mode first. It explains most surprises.

articles.title: Move and Transform
articles.summary: Move (V) drags artwork, and Transform (Ctrl+T) resizes and rotates it. Both work on a layer, and Transform can also move the pattern or base of a zone.
articles.what: In LAYER mode, click a sponsor or number with Move and drag it. Alt forces the whole layer to move. Pick (Y) isolates a single item inside a layer. Xform and the Transform menu open a free transform: drag the handles to resize, drag outside the box to rotate, press Enter to commit or Esc to cancel. The transform bar offers 90 degree turns each way, 180 degrees and Apply. Fit Layer to Zone Selection scales the selected artwork to sit inside the active zone mask. In ZONE mode Transform works on the zone's current pattern or base. Zone Pick lets you move, rotate and resize one pattern piece on its own. The transform box fits the layer's artwork, not the whole 2048 sheet. A live text layer stays text when you scale or rotate it; stretching, flipping or skewing it turns it into pixels (Ctrl+Z brings the text back). Smart guides: while you drag a layer or a piece, it snaps to the canvas edges and centre, to other layers and to your selection, with coloured guide lines; hold Ctrl for a free move or Shift for a straight line. In Move the arrow keys nudge 1 pixel, or 10 with Shift. Move on a live text layer moves the whole layer, and a double-click on it with Move opens the text for editing. deep.heading: Move picks a piece, not the whole layer
deep.body: In LAYER mode, clicking a sponsor, number or shape with Move (V) isolates just that piece with a tight box so you can move, rotate and scale it on its own. Hold Alt to force the whole layer to move instead. Outside LAYER mode, Ctrl+drag moves the layer. Pick (Y) does the same isolation without any dragging side effects. A live text layer is the exception: Move always moves the whole text layer, and a double-click on it with Move opens the text for editing. A piece you picked shows the label Just this piece with the hint Enter or double-click = done, Esc = cancel.

deep.heading: Resize and rotate with the handles
deep.body: Xform (Ctrl+T) opens a transform box. Drag a corner handle to resize. Hold Shift on a corner to keep the proportions, or use the aspect lock so proportions stay locked without holding a key. Hold Alt on a corner to scale from the centre. Drag outside the box to rotate, and hold Shift to snap to 15 degree steps; on a single number or sponsor the snap also prefers 0, 90, 180 and 270 so text stays upright.

deep.heading: Keyboard fine control
deep.body: While a transform is open, the arrow keys move it 1 px, or 10 px with Shift. Alt+Arrow rotates 1 degree, or 5 degrees with Shift. Press R, S or X and Y to type an exact rotation, scale or position. Enter commits, Esc cancels, and in a zone transform a double-click applies it. Picking another tool mid-transform commits what you have. In the Move tool the arrow keys also nudge a whole layer, 1 px or 10 px with Shift, and a burst of presses is one undo step.

deep.heading: Zone transform moves a finish, not artwork
deep.body: In ZONE mode Xform acts on the zone's current pattern or base, so you can resize and rotate how a pattern sits on the car. Zone Pick (in the SELECT menu) lets you grab one spec pattern piece or base and give it its own move, rotate and proportional resize.

faq.q: How do I keep proportions while resizing?
faq.a: Drag a corner handle while holding Shift, or turn on the aspect lock so it stays on.

faq.q: How do I rotate in exact steps?
faq.a: Hold Shift while rotating to snap to 15 degrees, or press Alt+Arrow to nudge 1 degree (5 with Shift).

faq.q: How do I type exact numbers?
faq.a: With a transform open press R for rotation, S for scale, or X and Y for position, then enter the value.

faq.q: Move grabbed the whole layer. How do I pick one item?
faq.a: Use Pick (Y), or click without holding Alt. Alt forces the whole layer on purpose.

faq.q: How do I undo a transform?
faq.a: Press Esc before committing, or Ctrl+Z after.

faq.q: Why does dropping a file on the canvas replace my paint?
faq.a: A dropped file loads as the new source paint. To add a logo as artwork use Actions > Place image... instead.

faq.q: How do I line things up or centre them?
faq.a: Drag with Move (V). Magenta, cyan and yellow guide lines show when the piece lines up with another layer, the canvas or your selection. See Smart guides.

faq.q: What does Just this piece mean?
faq.a: You picked one piece of a layer instead of the whole layer. Press Enter or double-click to finish it, or Esc to cancel. Hold Alt to move the whole layer instead.

faq.q: Can I move a text layer?
faq.a: Yes. Drag it anywhere with Move (V) and the whole text moves as one. Double-click it with Move to edit the words.

mistakes.fix: Press Esc to cancel and drag a corner with Shift held, or switch on the aspect lock.

mistakes.symptom: I changed tools and my transform vanished
mistakes.cause: Switching tools mid-transform commits it.
mistakes.fix: Press Ctrl+Z to undo the commit and reopen the transform.

protips: Alt+Arrow rotation nudges work for both layers and zone patterns, so you can fix a one-degree lean without touching the mouse.
With the aspect lock on, corner handles stay proportional for the whole session without a held key.
On Numbers layers the Shift rotation snap prefers upright angles, so numbers do not end up tilted by 3 degrees.

articles.title: Mirror Mask, Mirror Clone and symmetry
articles.summary: Mirror tools copy your work to the other side. Mirror Paint copies your strokes as you paint, and the Car menu copies a finished design; Mirror Mask and the layer MIRROR button flip a zone area or a layer.
articles.what: Mirror Mask (in the MASK menu and the selection bar) flips the active zone mask horizontally (left to right). On a layer card, MIRROR duplicates the layer and flips it to the opposite side of the car, which is the quick way to make a matching sponsor on the other door. FLIP H and FLIP V flip a layer in place, and ROT 90 turns it. Because the paint is the car laid flat, one side of the car can sit upside down on the sheet, so always check the result on the preview. There is also a Car menu in the toolbar: Mirror Paint copies every Brush, Eraser and Retouch stroke to the matching part of the car as you paint, Mirror To Other Side and Copy To Other Side (Text Reads Right) copy a layer or selection fitted to the other panel, and Car Stripe... adds a centre stripe. The Car menu also has Number Kit (the car number on both doors and the roof), Sponsor Kit (one logo on many parts) and Car-Space Fade (a fade along the car); see the Car menu article.

A zone area should be the same on both halves.
how: 1. For a layer: click MIRROR on its layer card, then use FLIP or ROT 90 if the copy lands upside down.
2. For a zone area: select the zone and press Mirror in the selection bar, or Mirror Mask in the MASK menu.
3. Check the CAR view to confirm the copy is on the right side.

deep.heading: Everything mirrors around the middle of the sheet
deep.body: Both mirror tools flip across the vertical centre line of the whole 2048 pixel sheet, not around the middle of the thing you selected. Mirror Mask swaps every pixel with the one in the same row on the opposite side of the sheet. Mirror on a layer card copies the layer and places the flipped copy at the mirrored position, so something at the far left lands at the far right. A graphic that sits near the middle of the sheet barely moves.

deep.heading: Mirror Mask versus Copy Mask
deep.body: Mirror Mask flips the selected zone's own mask in place, and the app tells you if the mask is already symmetric and nothing changed. Copy Mask is different: it sends the selected zone's mask to another zone, replacing that zone's mask, and says so if both are already identical. Use Copy Mask first, then Mirror Mask on the copy, to make a left-right pair of zones.

deep.heading: What Mirror Clone makes
deep.body: The MIRROR button on a layer card makes a new layer named after the original with (mirror) added. The copy is a horizontal flip with the same opacity, blend mode, visibility and clipping as the original, and it is a separate layer you can reorder, move or delete. Text flipped this way reads backwards, so retype or flip it back for lettering that must read correctly.

deep.heading: Flat sheet means odd results
deep.body: The sheet is the car laid flat, and one side of the car is often stored upside down. A plain left-right flip therefore sometimes puts the copy on the right panel but upside down. Fix it with FLIP V or ROT 90 on the layer card. ROT 90 turns the layer 90 degrees clockwise each press.

faq.a: One side of the car is stored upside down on the sheet. Press FLIP V or ROT 90 on the copy until it reads correctly on the car.

faq.q: What is the difference between FLIP H and MIRROR?

articles.title: Undo, redo and history
articles.summary: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes. For a longer trail, open Undo History and step back several actions.
articles.what: Undo takes back the last stroke, transform or layer action. Redo (Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z) puts it back. The HISTORY menu in the toolbar also has Undo, Redo and Undo History, which shows the recent actions with what each one was; you step back with Undo. Every answer from the AI copilot is one undo step for the zones it changed (plus one per layer it changed), and the Undo button under its answer reverses all of it. RENDER HISTORY is separate: it keeps thumbnails of past renders you can rebuild.

You want to compare an earlier look.

2. Press Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) to redo.
3. For many steps, open HISTORY > Undo History and keep pressing Undo.

deep.heading: One trail, four memories
deep.body: Ctrl+Z walks back through one list of actions, but the app keeps four different memories behind it, each with its own depth. Where a zone's painted area is concerned it keeps the last 60 steps. Zone settings (base, pattern, intensity, adding or deleting a zone) keep the last 15. Pixel painting on the source image keeps only the last 6, because each step is a full 2048 by 2048 picture. Layer edits keep between 5 and 30 steps, depending on how much memory their snapshots take, with a budget of about 96 MB.

deep.heading: What shows in Undo History
deep.body: HISTORY, Undo History opens a side panel listing recent actions from all four memories in the order you did them. The list is capped at 200 entries. Each entry carries a short label such as Zone 2 edit or a named layer action, so you can see what you are about to step back through.

deep.heading: Redo disappears when you do something new
deep.body: Redo is Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z. The moment you make a fresh change after undoing, the redo trail is cleared, as in most editors. Redoing step by step keeps the remaining redo steps alive. So if you undo three times and want to look, redo them all before you touch anything.

deep.heading: Undo versus Render History
deep.body: Undo reverses edits to your zones, masks and layers. RENDER HISTORY is a separate list of past renders shown as thumbnails you can rebuild from. Clearing Undo History empties the list and cannot itself be undone.

faq.q: How many undos do I get?
faq.a: It depends on what you did. Zone area edits keep 60 steps, zone settings 15, pixel painting 6, and layer edits between 5 and 30.

faq.q: Why can I not undo further after painting a lot?
faq.a: Pixel painting on the source image keeps only the 6 most recent steps because each one is a whole-picture snapshot. Work on a layer or use zones when you need a deep history.

faq.q: Where is the redo shortcut?
faq.a: Ctrl+Y, or Ctrl+Shift+Z. The HISTORY menu and right-click menu also have Redo.

faq.q: Did the AI copilot change my zones and can I reverse it?
faq.a: Yes. Each answer counts as one undo step for the zones it changed, plus one per layer. The Undo button under its answer reverses all of it at once.

faq.q: Can I undo Clear in Undo History?
faq.a: No. Clear wipes the list and that action itself cannot be undone.

faq.q: Is Render History the same as Undo?
faq.a: No. Render History keeps thumbnails of past renders; Undo steps back your edits.

mistakes.fix: Paint on a layer instead, or save a project copy before big experiments.

articles.title: Zoom and pan
articles.summary: Zoom changes the editor view, not the artwork pixels or exported image size. Current extended zoom controls reach 3200 percent. The wheel can instead resize an active zone placement target; use the zoom buttons or leave placement editing when you only want to change the view.
articles.what: Normal canvas zoom changes displayed canvas width and height through CSS, using the canvas pixel dimensions times the view zoom. It does not resize the source image buffer. Current extended plus/minus controls have steps through 3200 percent, while the ordinary unrotated/unflipped wheel path zooms continuously within 10–3200 percent. FIT fits the view with a 10-percent floor and 100-percent ceiling; 1:1 sets 100 percent. Wheel scrolling is not always view-only: a selected zone with an active placement target can route the wheel to placement scale, push a Scale placement undo entry and trigger a preview. If that happens, inspect the placement/history rather than assuming the artwork itself was resized.
when: You need to see fine detail on a number or edge.
You are lost and want the whole car back.
how: For view-only magnification, use the canvas zoom buttons or shortcuts. Inspect placement mode before using the wheel.
Use FIT for the whole sheet or 1:1 for 100-percent view.
To pan, use the documented hand/middle-button workflow; do not confuse view navigation with moving a layer.
If scrolling changed a finish or pattern placement, inspect that target and the Scale placement history entry. Changing the view is a separate operation from artwork transformation.

faq.a: The current extended zoom controls reach 3200 percent. The older 400-percent answer described the previous ladder. Ordinary unrotated/unflipped wheel zoom is continuous within 10–3200 percent; other view modes and compatibility paths can differ.

faq.q: Why did my pattern resize when I scrolled?
faq.a: A placement target was active with a zone selected, so the wheel scaled the placement by 5 percent per tick. Leave placement mode or use Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- to zoom.

faq.q: How do I pan without holding Space?
faq.a: Drag with the middle mouse button.

faq.q: What does FIT do on a big monitor?
faq.a: It fits the paint to the window but stops at 100 percent, so it never blows the paint up past actual size.

faq.q: Why do the 1 and 2 keys change my layer opacity?
faq.a: In LAYER mode with a layer selected, number keys set layer opacity. Use the 1:1 button instead.

faq.q: What does Edit Big do?
faq.a: It hides the live preview so the source canvas can use the whole area. Click it again to bring the preview back.

faq.q: How do I zoom in on the canvas?
faq.a: Zoom and pan controls: scroll the wheel over the canvas, or use the keyboard shortcuts Ctrl+= to zoom in, Ctrl+- to zoom out and Ctrl+0 to fit the window; hold Space and drag, or drag with the middle mouse button, to pan. If the wheel resizes your pattern instead, a zone with a placement target is selected: leave placement mode or use the keys.

faq.q: Does zooming resize my artwork or exported paint?
faq.a: Normal view zoom changes CSS display size, not the source image dimensions or pixels. Artwork transforms and resizing are separate. An active zone placement target can intercept the wheel and change placement scale, so check that mode before assuming scrolling was view-only.

faq.q: My number looks smaller after zooming out. Did its layer shrink?
faq.a: A smaller view alone does not mean the number layer changed. Normal canvas zoom changes display size. Check the actual layer/image dimensions before resizing artwork; wheel placement editing is a separate exception.

faq.q: Why does scrolling change the finish instead of zooming?
faq.a: The wheel can route to the active placement target on a selected zone. That path changes placement scale and can record Scale placement in history. Leave placement editing or use the canvas zoom controls when you want view-only magnification.

faq.q: Should I undo an artwork resize just because I changed the view?
faq.a: First check what actually changed. Normal canvas zoom does not resize artwork. Inspect history and actual image/layer dimensions; active placement scrolling can change a finish target, while a separate artwork transform changes the artwork itself.

articles.summary: A short list of keys covers most of the work, and the question-mark key shows the full list inside the app.

Zones: Shift+N new, Shift+D duplicate, Shift+R randomise, Shift+E show or hide the zone panel, Alt+1 to 9 select a zone, Ctrl+Up / Down change priority. Render: Ctrl+R. deep.body: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste pixels, and Ctrl+Shift+V pastes in place. Ctrl+J makes a new layer from a copy of the selection and Ctrl+Shift+J from a cut. Delete removes selected pixels. Alt+Backspace fills the selection with your foreground colour and Ctrl+Backspace with the background colour. Ctrl+Shift+N adds a blank layer, Ctrl+Shift+E merges all visible layers, and Ctrl+Shift+R reloads the last paint file. articles.title: Clipping masks, clone stamp, flip, rotate, scale, crop and how many undos
articles.summary: Transform (Ctrl+T) moves, scales and rotates a layer, and Restrict to Layers is the nearest thing to a clipping mask; there is no crop or whole-design flip, and undo keeps up to 30 layer steps. Smart objects are not guaranteed to come back from Photoshop, so rasterise or flatten them first.
articles.what: Shokker is a paint booth, not a full photo editor. Artwork lives on layers: Transform (Ctrl+T) resizes and rotates the selected layer (with 90 and 180 degree buttons), the layer card has FLIP H and FLIP V, and the transform tools have Flip H and Flip V. There is no button that flips, rotates, scales or crops the whole paint at once (the right-click menu's Flip View H / Flip View V only mirror how you see the canvas, to check symmetry, and change no pixels), because the paint must stay the car's own 2048 x 2048 template layout. There is no clipping mask either: to keep a finish inside one piece of artwork, restrict the zone to that layer. To keep brush and retouch paint inside a zone, tick Clip to <zone> in the tool options bar. The RETOUCH menu has a Clone Stamp (S): Alt+click a clean spot to set the source, then paint. The Healing Brush (J) does the same but blends the repair into the colours around it. Undo depth differs by kind of change: 60 steps for selections and masks, up to 30 for layer edits (fewer, down to 5, when the edits are large, because layer history has a memory budget), 15 for zone settings and 6 for brush strokes. Smart objects and live Photoshop text are not plain pixels, so a round trip through Photoshop does not guarantee they come back editable: rasterise or flatten them in Photoshop first, then open the file again.
when: You look for a Photoshop tool such as clipping mask, clone stamp or crop.
You want to flip, rotate or resize artwork.
You undid too far or want to know how far back you can go.
how: 1. Select the layer in the LAYERS column and switch the toolbar to LAYER.
2. Press Ctrl+T (Transform) to drag, scale and rotate it; use the 90 / 180 degree buttons for exact turns, then Apply.
3. To mirror artwork, press FLIP H or FLIP V on the layer card, or Flip H / Flip V while transforming.
4. To keep a finish inside one piece of artwork (like a clipping mask), open the zone's COLOR section and tick that layer under RESTRICT TO LAYERS.
5. To repair artwork, open RETOUCH and use the Healing Brush: Alt+click a clean spot, then paint over the flaw.
tips: Open Undo History to see every change listed newest first and jump back several steps at once.
pitfalls: FLIP H and FLIP V on the layer card change the layer's pixels; the transform Flip H / Flip V is non-destructive until you apply it.
Brush strokes keep only 6 undo steps, because each one is a full 2048 x 2048 snapshot; save before a long retouch.

deep.heading: Why there is no whole-paint flip, scale or crop
deep.body: iRacing only accepts a 2048 x 2048 (or 1024 x 1024) paint laid out exactly like the car's template. Flipping, rotating, scaling or cropping the whole sheet would move every panel off its place on the car, so Shokker edits artwork one layer at a time. Patterns and bases are laid flat on that sheet too: they can be tiled, fitted to the zone or placed and rotated by hand (Flip and Rotate 90 in the placement tools), but they do not bend to follow body panels.

deep.heading: How far back undo goes
deep.body: Each kind of change has its own history. Selections and zone masks keep 60 steps (they are compressed, so this costs little memory). Layer edits keep up to 30 (as few as 5 when the edits are big, because layer history is held to a memory budget). Zone settings such as base, pattern and intensity keep 15. Brush strokes keep 6, because each stroke stores a whole 2048 x 2048 picture. Ctrl+Z steps back, Ctrl+Y steps forward, and Undo History lets you jump.

faq.a: No. Tick the layer under RESTRICT TO LAYERS on the zone to keep a look inside that artwork.

faq.q: Where is the clone stamp?
faq.a: In the RETOUCH menu, or press S. Alt+click a clean spot to set the source, then paint. The Healing Brush (J) also blends the repair into the colours around it.

faq.q: Can I flip or rotate the whole design?
faq.a: No; flip or rotate one layer at a time with FLIP H / FLIP V or Transform (Ctrl+T). The right-click Flip View H / V only mirrors your view of the canvas.

faq.q: How many undos do I get?
faq.a: 60 selection steps, up to 30 layer steps (fewer for big edits), 15 zone steps and 6 brush strokes.

faq.q: Do Photoshop smart objects survive a round trip?
faq.a: Not guaranteed. Smart objects are not plain pixels, so they may not come back as editable layers. Rasterise or flatten them in Photoshop first, then open the file in Shokker again.

articles.title: Liquify, warp and bending artwork
articles.summary: Shokker has no Liquify, Warp or Puppet Warp tool. Transform (Ctrl+T) moves, scales and rotates a layer, and Smudge (Q) in the RETOUCH menu smears layer pixels; to bend a logo along a curve, do it in Photoshop and open the PSD again.
articles.what: Shokker's editing tools work on flat layers. Transform (Ctrl+T) in LAYER mode moves, scales and rotates the selected artwork. The RETOUCH menu has twelve tools, among them Color Brush, Recolor, Healing Brush, Smudge and Burn. Smudge smears the selected layer's pixels in the direction you drag, with its own Strength from 1 to 100 percent (50 to start); it can push an edge a little, but it is not a warp mesh. There is no tool that bends, curves or distorts a whole logo. For that, warp the artwork in Photoshop or another editor, save the PSD and open it again with Open Paint... > Layered template in the top row.
when: You want to bend a logo round a wheel arch or along a stripe.
You look for Photoshop's Liquify, Warp or Puppet Warp.
Artwork needs a small push or stretch.
how: 1. To move, resize or turn artwork, select its layer, switch the toolbar to LAYER and press Ctrl+T (Transform). Drag, scale and rotate, then Apply.
2. For a small push of pixels, open RETOUCH, pick Smudge (Q), set Strength and drag on the layer.
3. To bend artwork properly, warp it in Photoshop or another editor and save the PSD.
4. Open it again in Shokker with Open Paint... > Layered template in the top row, or add the bent logo as a transparent PNG with Actions > Place image...
tips: Smudge at low Strength with several short strokes looks cleaner than one long stroke.
Remember the sheet is flat: a straight logo on the sheet already follows the panel on the car.
pitfalls: Smudge smears texture as well as shape, so fine detail goes soft.
Transform changes the selected artwork or selection as a whole; it cannot curve one part of it.

deep.heading: What each tool can do
deep.body: Transform changes position, size and angle of a whole layer or selection. Smudge drags pixels along your stroke. Healing Brush blends clean texture over a flaw. None of them bends a shape along a curve, which is what Liquify or Warp do in a photo editor.

deep.heading: The round trip for warped artwork
deep.body: Do the bending where the warp tools are, then bring the result back: save the layered PSD and open it with Open Paint... > Layered template, or export the bent logo as a transparent PNG and add it with Actions > Place image... Your zones and finishes stay in the Shokker project.

articles.title: Shine Lens: see how your finish catches the light
articles.summary: The Shine bar under the Live Preview shows your finish under a studio light, so you can see chrome, satin, candy and carbon shine before you render. It is a preview only and changes nothing.
articles.what: Under the Live Preview there is a small Shine bar with Off, Lens, Full and Sweep. Lens puts a light circle under your mouse. Full lights the whole preview. Sweep makes the light circle the car by itself. You can also hold the ` key (top left, under Esc) over the car for a quick peek with any tool. The lens shows the spec map the preview already made, so it never renders, never changes your files and costs no time.
when: You want to know if a finish is mirror, satin or matte before you render.
Flake, candy or chrome looks flat in the normal preview.
You are comparing two finishes and want the same light on both.
how: 1. Find the small Shine bar under the Live Preview.
2. Click Lens and move the mouse over the Live Preview. A circle shows that spot under a studio light.
3. Click Full to light the whole preview, then drag on the car (or drag the little round light button at the end of the bar) to move the light. The arrow keys nudge it too.
4. Click Sweep and the light circles the car by itself. This is the best way to check flake, candy and chrome.
5. For a quick look while another tool is active, hold the ` key over the car. Let go and the circle disappears. Click Off to go back to the normal flat preview.

tips: Sharp, bright stripes mean mirror-smooth (low roughness). A soft, wide glow means satin. Nothing moving means matte or no clearcoat.
Peek anywhere: the ` key works with whatever tool you have, so you do not need to switch to Lens.
pitfalls: The lens is a preview under a studio light. iRacing lights the car with the track sky and sun, so use the lens to compare finishes and then check the car in the sim.
If you have just changed a finish, wait for the Live Preview to update before you judge the lens.

deep.heading: What the lens really shows
deep.body: The lens does not render a new picture. It takes the spec map that the Live Preview has already made, with the metal, roughness and clearcoat of every pixel, and lights it with a studio light on your screen. That is why it is instant and why it can never change your TGA files. The spec map has four channels: red is metallic, green is roughness (0 is a mirror, but only chrome-tier metal, about 240 and up, can go under 15), blue is clearcoat (0 to 15 is none, 16 is maximum gloss, 255 is dull) and alpha is the mask. If something looks wrong in the lens, it will look wrong in iRacing too.

deep.heading: How to read the light
deep.body: Sharp, bright stripes that slide across the panel mean mirror-smooth metal, with roughness (green) near 0. A soft, wide glow means satin, a medium roughness. Nothing moving as the light passes means matte, a high roughness, or no clearcoat (blue between 0 and 15). Candy and carbon sparkle because their fine texture catches the light at many small angles.

deep.heading: Lens, Full, Sweep and Peek
deep.body: Lens lights a circle under the mouse and leaves the rest of the preview flat. Full lights the whole preview from a light you place by dragging on the car, by dragging the round light button, or with the arrow keys. Sweep moves that light around the car on its own. Peek is the ` key: hold it and a circle follows the mouse whatever tool you have, let go and it is gone.

deep.heading: Material, not colour
deep.body: The Magic Wand picks by colour. Select > Material... picks by the spec map: how metallic, how rough and how much clearcoat each pixel has. The spec map has four channels: red is metallic, green is roughness (0 is a mirror, but only chrome-tier metal, about 240 and up, can go under 15), blue is clearcoat (0 to 15 is none, 16 is maximum gloss, 255 is dull) and alpha is the mask. So a red chrome panel and a blue chrome panel both count as chrome.

deep.heading: Tolerance, Soft Edge and Match Whole Finish
deep.body: Tolerance (0 to 80, starts at 12) decides how different a pixel can be and still match. Soft Edge (0 to 64, starts at 6) feathers the edge of the selection. Match Whole Finish looks at small neighbourhoods instead of single pixels, so a finish with fine texture counts as one material. Contiguous keeps only the patch that touches the spot you clicked.

deep.heading: Presets and Apply As
deep.body: All Chrome, All Matte and All Gloss Clear need no click. Rough Below N picks everything with roughness (green) under N. Metal Above N picks everything with metal (red) over N. Apply As chooses how the result joins the current Zone selection: Replace swaps it, Add joins it and Subtract removes it.

articles.title: Material Brush: put a real finish on the car
articles.summary: The Material Brush paints any Shokker finish, such as chrome, candy or a flake, straight onto the car by hand. RENDER writes it into your paint and spec files.
articles.what: Open the Material / Spec menu in the toolbar (next to Retouch) or press U. Click the finish button in the bar above the canvas, pick any finish from the normal finish picker, then brush it on. The brush uses the usual Size, Opacity and Hardness. Soft edges and lower opacity really blend, so a 50 percent chrome stroke renders as half chrome. The Source view shows your stroke at once, and a moment later the Live Preview shows the real finish made by the engine.
when: You want chrome, candy or a flake on one spot only, such as a roof stripe or a mirror cap.
You want to paint a finish by hand instead of making a Zone for it.
how: 1. Open the Material / Spec menu in the toolbar (next to Retouch) or press U.
2. In the bar above the canvas, click the finish button (it shows the current finish, for example Chrome) and pick any finish in the finish picker.
3. Set Size, Opacity and Hardness, then brush it onto the car.
4. Watch the Source view for your stroke. A moment later the Live Preview shows the real finish.
5. Hold Alt and brush to erase the material. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo one stroke at a time. Press RENDER when you are happy.

deep.heading: What the brush really writes
deep.body: Each finish you brush is a coat the engine makes with the same maths as a Zone finish. RENDER writes the stroke into the paint TGA and the spec TGA, so iRacing gets exactly what the Live Preview showed. deep.heading: Soft edges and opacity
deep.body: Hardness and Opacity blend the finish in step by step. A 50 percent chrome stroke gives half the metal of full chrome, so it reads as satin chrome, not as a half-covered patch. Use a soft, low-opacity stroke to fade chrome into the paint around it.

deep.heading: Zones, erasing and undo
deep.body: If a Zone with an area is selected, strokes stay inside it unless you untick Clip to. Alt plus a stroke erases the Material from that spot. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo one whole stroke at a time, exactly.

articles.what: Open the Material / Spec menu or press Shift+U until the Spec Brush is active. 2. Pick a preset: Gloss, Satin, Matte, Chrome, Brushed Metal, Patina or Clearcoat Fade. Or type values from 0 to 255 in the M, R and CC boxes.
3. Click a letter (M, R or CC) to switch that channel off and leave it alone.
4. Brush over the panel. For Brushed Metal or Patina, turn on Grain for fine texture that follows your stroke.

deep.heading: What M, R and CC mean

The spec map has four channels: red is metallic, green is roughness (0 is a mirror, but only chrome-tier metal, about 240 and up, can go under 15), blue is clearcoat (0 to 15 is none, 16 is maximum gloss, 255 is dull) and alpha is the mask.

deep.heading: Presets and the numbers behind them

After a stroke the bottom bar shows the values read back from the car (on car: M, R, CC), so you can see what iRacing will get.

articles.title: Wear Brush: race wear painted by hand
articles.summary: The Wear Brush writes real race wear into both the paint and the spec in one stroke: dirt and grime, rubber marks and stone chips.
articles.what: Open the Material / Spec menu or press Shift+U until you reach the Wear Brush. Pick Dirt / Grime, Rubber Marks or Stone Chips and stroke it onto the car. Dirt gives brown-grey streaks that follow your stroke, and the surface goes dull and rough. Rubber Marks gives dark tyre-rubber marbles and rub streaks, matte. Stone Chips gives small irregular chips, each with a bare-metal core, a primer ring and a dark lip. The texture is fine, about 8 to 32 pixels, so it reads as real wear on the whole car.
when: You want a raced-hard look with this brush, such as grime low on the doors or rubber on the fenders.
You want chips on the nose and hood edge.
how: 1. Open the Material / Spec menu or press Shift+U until you reach the Wear Brush.
2. Pick the wear type: Dirt / Grime, Rubber Marks or Stone Chips.
3. Set Size and Opacity, then stroke along the way the air flows over the car, from the nose toward the rear.
4. Check the Live Preview. The Shine Lens shows the dull, rough dirt and the shiny bare-metal chip cores.
5. Ctrl+Z undoes a stroke. Press RENDER when you like it.

deep.body: Dirt and grime follow the direction you stroke, so they look like spray and airflow. Stroke from the nose toward the rear, or upward from the sills, and the streaks match how real dirt lies on a race car.
